Here's a strange fact: you have never seen your own face. Not really. You've seen reflections, which are reversed. You've seen photographs, which flatten and freeze. But the face the world meets—the one that flushes when you're embarrassed, that crumples when you laugh—exists only for other people. Everyone you've ever loved knows your face better than you do.

The part of you most "you" is invisible to you. You live behind your eyes, looking out, and the face everyone reads is one you can never fully inspect.

Mirrors complicate things further. When you look in a mirror, you hold still. You compose yourself. You see your "mirror face," the arranged version. Meanwhile, strangers catch you mid-sneeze, mid-reverie, mid-giggle. They know the unguarded you, the you that exists when you forget anyone's watching.

Maybe this is why photographs of ourselves so often feel wrong. "That doesn't look like me," we say—meaning it doesn't look like the person in the mirror, the only version we've ever known. But the mirror image is reversed. In a sense, the photograph is more accurate. The discomfort is the feeling of meeting yourself as a stranger.

I find this oddly comforting. We contain versions of ourselves we cannot access, and the people around us hold pieces we'll never see. We're stored in each other—fragments of face, gesture, laugh, scattered across everyone who has ever looked at us with attention.

You will never see yourself whole. But you are seen.

I find this oddly comforting. We contain versions of ourselves we cannot access, and the people around us hold pieces we'll never see. We're stored in each other—fragments of face, gesture, laugh, scattered across everyone who has ever looked at us with attention.

You will never see yourself whole. But you are seen.
